newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Spies make HK unattractive military base for China.
newsitem.headline: Spies make HK unattractive military base for China.

text.p: Hong Kong is the worst possible place for China to develop into a major military base, partly because it is such a hotbed of spying, a leading China-watcher said on Thursday.

Freewheeling Hong Kong has long been the most active centre for intelligence gathering in the region and this activity is likely to increase after the handover of the British colony at midnight on June 30, said Gerald Segal, senior fellow at the International Institute of Strategic Studies in London.
Hong Kong would in theory be ideally placed geographically for the Chinese navy to keep watch on Taiwan and for potential conflicts in the South China Sea over disputed island chains.

"The reality is, though, that because this place is such a strong civilian port it is possibly the worst possible place to base a significant military force," the scholar told a Foreign Correspondents' Club briefing.

The Taiwan crisis last year, when China conducted serious war games close to Taiwan, underlined that China, like most armed forces, seeks to close ports when it is conducting military operations, the London-based scholar said.
"Closing the port is obviously not a military option for Hong Kong," he said.
The British navy had made only 14 port visits to Hong Kong over the past five years, he said.

"This tells you a little bit how irrelevant this place is from the British military view and therefore it is not surprising that the Chinese won't base significant military forces here in the short terms and probably the long term. They have other facilities in the region."
The Chinese navy would be unlikely to risk attracting the attention of the extensive spying networks in place in Hong Kong.

"It has been one of the truisms about this place over the last 30 or 40 years that it has been a place, perhaps the place in East Asia, where intelligence agencies of various governments have operated and spied on each other," Segal said.

"It is no secret that western governments have made attempts to leave assets of a human and a physical kind in this place over the handover period and therefore there is a reasonable expectation that the Chinese authorities and their supporters will seek ways to uncover these people and technology."

Segal said the spying did not comprise just the west spying on China and vice versa but also what he called "inter-Chinese" spying -- provinces, ministries, and even factions within the People's Liberation Army, spying on each other from Hong Kong.
This intelligence activity needs to be watched -- particularly if the future administration conducts a series of witch-hunts which could reach proportions that may damage confidence, he said.
